Note: The user running the code needs to update file paths. The data that is retrieved comes in the form of a text file and is saved into the “inputs” folder. Subsequent code writes the data to csv files into the “outputs2” folder.

https://api.census.gov/data/2018/zbp/variables.html


https://api.census.gov/data/2017/zbp/variables.html


https://api.census.gov/data/2016/zbp/variables.html

# Initialize variables for API request
dsource = 'zbp'
ecols = 'ESTAB,EMP,EMPSZES,GEO_ID,ZIPCODE,PAYQTR1,PAYANN'
api_key = 'da5ca696289b328bc3575a3405c6196767cb452c'
naics = '445310' # Note: You can update the NAICS code to import other industry data


# Updated to change census year depending on calendar year of data

# Define the path to the "input" folder relative to the user's home directory. 
# This is where the data retrieved from the API request will be stored.
user_home = os.path.expanduser("~")
input_folder = os.path.join(user_home, 'OneDrive - Colostate', 'Teaching', 'Courses', 'CSU', 'AREC570', 'api_docs', 'zbp_data', 'input')
print(input_folder)

# Define the mapping of years to nyear
year_to_nyear = {
    2000: 1997,
    2001: 1997,
    2002: 2002,
    2003: 2002,
    2004: 2002,
    2005: 2002,
    2006: 2002,
    2007: 2007,
    2008: 2007,
    2009: 2007,
    2010: 2007,
    2011: 2007,
    2012: 2012,
    2013: 2012,
    2014: 2012,
    2015: 2012,
    2016: 2012,
    2017: 2017,
    2018: 2017
}

# Loop through years and set nyear accordingly
for year in range(2000, 2019):
    nyear = year_to_nyear[year]
    base_url = f'https://api.census.gov/data/{year}/{dsource}'
    edata_url = f'{base_url}?get={ecols}&NAICS{nyear}={naics}&for=zipcode:*&key={api_key}'
    
    # Use edata_url for the desired API request or further processing
    print(f'For year {year}, nyear is {nyear}, and edata_url is: {edata_url}')
    
    # Make an API request, retrieve data, and save to a file
    a = requests.get(edata_url)
    quote = a.text
    outpath = os.path.join(input_folder, f'Out{year}_NAICS{naics}.txt')
    with open(outpath, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(quote)
        
    print(outpath)


# Specify the input folder and output folder
user_home = os.path.expanduser("~")
output_folder = os.path.join(user_home, 'OneDrive - Colostate', 'Teaching', 'Courses', 'CSU', 'AREC570', 'api_docs', 'zbp_data', 'output')
print(output_folder)

# Function to remove brackets from a list
def remove_brackets(lst):
    return [item.strip('[]"') for item in lst]

# Loop through the text files in the input folder
for filename in os.listdir(input_folder):
    if filename.endswith(".txt"):
        # Construct the full file paths
        input_file = os.path.join(input_folder, filename)
        output_file = os.path.join(output_folder, os.path.splitext(filename)[0] + ".csv")

        # Open the input text file for reading
        with open(input_file, 'r', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as txt_file:
            # Read the data from the text file and remove brackets
            data = [remove_brackets(row) for row in csv.reader(txt_file)]
            
            # Print the top 5 rows
            print(f'Top 5 rows of {filename}:')
            for row in data[:5]:
                print(row)

            # Open the corresponding output CSV file for writing
            with open(output_file, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as csv_file:
                # Write the data to the CSV file
                csv.writer(csv_file).writerows(data)

        print(f'Converted {filename} to {os.path.basename(output_file)}')

print("Conversion complete.")

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
The reviewer’s job
Help the editor assess the paper and help the author understand its strengths and weaknesses.

Identify the contribution.
Assess the evidence and reasoning.
Distinguish essential revisions from optional improvements.
Explain the recommendation.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Where the report fits
A typical sequence:

Submission and editorial screening.
Invitation to reviewers.
Reports and editorial decision.
Revision, rejection, or acceptance.

Procedures vary by journal. Follow the instructions for the specific review.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
section: Evaluate the paper in front of you
text:
Evaluate the paper in front of you

Engage with its question and intended contribution.
Do not require the author to write your preferred different paper.
Explain problems rather than merely declaring them.
Be direct and constructive.

Source: Berk et al. (2015).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
AJAE: several dimensions of merit
The assigned criteria address:

Contribution and originality.
Scholarship and analysis.
Appeal to the readership.
Appropriate illustrations and length.

A report should explain how the paper meets or falls short of relevant criteria.
Source: Agricultural and Applied Economics Association (2013).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Ethridge: follow the argument

Is the objective clear?
Does the sequence of ideas lead toward it?
Does the organization help the reader?
Are important terms precise and consistent?
Which general problem matters more than sentence-level edits?

Source: Ethridge (2004).

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Discussion: identify the binding weakness
A paper has a clear question, polished prose, and precise estimates, but its comparison group is exposed to the treatment.

Which review criterion is affected?
Why does the concern matter?
What evidence or revision could address it?
When would this be fatal to the paper’s main claim?

Hypothetical review exercise.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Structure a referee report

Brief summary of question, method, and main contribution.
Overall assessment.
Major comments, ordered by importance.
Specific comments with locations.
Recommendation communicated as the journal requests.

A summary demonstrates understanding; it should not dominate the report.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Make a major comment actionable
A strong comment contains:

Concern: what is wrong or unclear?
Consequence: how does it affect the conclusion?
Remedy: what analysis or explanation could resolve it?
Priority: is it essential?

Avoid an unexplained list of preferred robustness checks.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Exercise: revise a weak comment

The empirical strategy is unconvincing. Add more controls.

Rewrite it to identify:

The potential confounder.
Why it threatens the interpretation.
A feasible diagnostic or revision.
What remains uncertain even after that revision.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research
text:
Discussion: Berk, Harvey, and Hirshleifer

How can a reviewer distinguish an essential change from an optional suggestion?
What makes a recommendation useful to an editor?
Why can unnecessary revision requests slow scientific progress?
How should a reviewer handle limits to their own expertise?

Research merit.

title: Lecture 7.1: Reviewing Research

section: Separate the target from the tool
text:
Separate the target from the tool

Estimand: the quantity we want to learn.
Estimator: the rule used to estimate it from data.
Estimate: the numerical result in our sample.

Example: an average treatment effect, a difference-in-means estimator, and its estimated value.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
What creates a credible comparison?
For every design, ask:

Who is compared with whom?
What creates the difference in treatment?
What must be true of the untreated counterfactual?
To which population does the result apply?

Source: Athey and Imbens (2017).

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Regression discontinuity
Treatment changes at a threshold in a running variable.

Compare observations close to the cutoff.
Ask whether other determinants of the outcome change smoothly.
Check for manipulation and other policies at the same threshold.
Interpret the effect locally.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Sharp and fuzzy designs

Sharp RD: treatment status changes deterministically at the threshold.
Fuzzy RD: the probability of treatment changes.

In a fuzzy design, divide the outcome discontinuity by the treatment discontinuity, with additional assumptions for a local causal interpretation.
A weak treatment discontinuity makes inference difficult.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Difference-in-differences
τ̂=(Y‾T,post−Y‾T,pre)−(Y‾C,post−Y‾C,pre)
\hat\tau =
(\bar Y_{T,\mathrm{post}}-\bar Y_{T,\mathrm{pre}})
-
(\bar Y_{C,\mathrm{post}}-\bar Y_{C,\mathrm{pre}})

The comparison group supplies a counterfactual change.
The key assumption concerns parallel untreated trends, not identical outcome levels.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Assess the DiD argument

Why should untreated trends be comparable?
Are there anticipatory responses?
Did another policy change at the same time?
Did group composition change?
Could treatment spill over to the comparison group?

Similar pre-trends are useful evidence, not proof of the identifying assumption.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Synthetic control
Construct a weighted comparison from untreated units.

Choose weights using pre-intervention information.
Assess pre-intervention fit.
Examine the post-intervention gap.
Investigate donor contamination and sensitivity.

A close pre-treatment fit does not by itself establish causality.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:

A policy begins in one region, with several years of data before and after.

What would support DiD?

Would a threshold design be available?

Do not select a method only because software can estimate it.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation
text:
Placebos probe specific threats
A placebo asks whether the design finds an effect where the proposed mechanism predicts none.
Examples:

A false treatment date before the intervention.
An outcome that should not respond.
Predetermined characteristics at an RD cutoff.

Explain why each placebo is informative.

Preserves the lottery example from source slide 38: compare large and small prize winners, then ask whether future winnings predict pre-treatment earnings. For RD, examine discontinuities in predetermined covariates rather than requiring unconditional independence from treatment.

title: Lecture 6.2: Causality and Policy Evaluation

Change a justified modeling or design choice and explain what that change tests.

Alternative bandwidth.
Alternative comparison group.
Alternative measurement.
Alternative functional form.

Report informative disagreements. Avoid searching for a specification that preserves a preferred result.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Reading and sequence
Champ, “Collecting Nonmarket Valuation Data” (Champ 2017)

Choose between primary and secondary data
Define the population frame and sampling approach
Translate the desired measures into survey questions
Select the mode and fieldwork procedures
Process and document the completed data


Champ presents these as connected decisions shaped by the research objective budget time and available labor. The lecture follows that sequence using one illustrative nonmarket valuation study.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Example: valuing a river restoration program
text:
Example: valuing a river restoration program
A county is considering restoration of ten miles of a local river to improve water quality habitat and recreation
The program would be funded by an annual household fee for five years
Research objective: Estimate county households’ willingness to pay for the specified program

This is a classroom example rather than a description of a proposed local policy. Keep the policy fixed throughout the lecture so that changes in the population frame question and mode can be interpreted against the same objective.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
What is the data required?
Look at the objective to determine the data requirement: Estimate county households’ willingness to pay for the specified program
The study needs information about:

Conditions without the program
The environmental change produced by the program
Household choices when the program and payment are presented together
Characteristics used to interpret differences in those choices

Other options wouldn’t allow you to achieve the objective:

Water monitoring data
Visitation records


These do not directly reveal choices for a program that does not yet exist.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Primary and secondary data







Primary data
Secondary data




Collected directly for the current study
Existing data reused for the current study


Instrument timing and recruitment can be tailored
Existing documentation design and variables set the limits


Research team controls and bears responsibility for collection
Research team must reconstruct provenance and fitness for use


Usually requires more time money and administration
Can reduce cost time and respondent burden



Suitability depends on the question population measure and intended inference

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
When is each source appropriate?
Primary data are useful when

The required construct is absent from existing data
The policy or choice is hypothetical
The study requires tailored timing questions or recruitment


Secondary data are useful when

Existing measures correspond to the required concepts
The population units timing and definitions fit the study
Provenance and data-generating procedures can be assessed

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Apply the distinction to our river study example
text:
Apply the distinction to our river study example








Source
Potential use
Limitation




Water-quality monitoring
Describe baseline conditions
Does not measure household preferences


Recreation counts
Measure observed site use
Misses nonusers and passive-use values


Property transactions
Study capitalization near the river
Represents housing-market choices


Household survey
Present the proposed program and payment
Quality depends on sampling and survey design

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Discussion: choose a source for your research
text:
Discussion: choose a source for your research
For your research project consider

Which concept(s) must be observed
Whether an existing source measures that concept
Whether its population timing unit and definition fit
What primary collection would add
Which limitation would remain after combining sources

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Data quality begins before the questionnaire
text:
Data quality begins before the questionnaire
Primer on non-market valuation addresses important concepts whether you’re collecting primary data or using secondary data.
A well-worded questionnaire cannot repair a frame that excludes part of the relevant population.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Who belongs in the river study population?
text:
Who belongs in the river study population?
Possible beneficiaries include

River users
Residents living near the river
County households that may pay the fee
Nonusers who value habitat preservation
People outside the county who visit or hold passive-use values

The policy question and payment jurisdiction determine which group the study is intended to represent

Champ emphasizes that passive-use values make geographic boundaries difficult. For this example use county households as the target population because they face the policy choice and payment. Other objectives would imply another population.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Population frame sample and respondents







Term
Example




Study population
County households whose values the study will represent


Sampling frame
Address list used to reach those households


Sample
Addresses selected from the frame


Respondents
Selected households that complete the survey



Inference becomes less reliable when movement from one row to the next is selective

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Probability and nonprobability sampling




Champ Figure 3.1. The first question is whether the study requires inference beyond the observed sample. Probability sampling gives each frame unit a known nonzero selection probability. Nonprobability recruitment does not.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Types of probability sampling designs
Use probability sampling when inference to a broader population is important.

Simple random sample
Every frame unit has the same probability of being chosen


Cluster sample
Select geographic groups first when in-person collection makes travel costly


Stratified random sample
Divides the sample frame into nonoverlapping subpopulations (strata) based on some measure available for the entire sample frame, e.g., sample separately by characteristics such as distance from the river or urban and rural location

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
When is nonprobability sampling appropriate?
When inference to a broader population is not important.
Convenience, purposive, and quota samples can support

Focus groups and cognitive interviews
Pilot testing
Method comparisons
Research restricted to the recruited participants

They do not provide known selection probabilities for population estimates

Champ cautions against generalizing beyond a nonprobability sample. Matching or weighting on observed demographics does not reveal how the sample differs on unobserved determinants of the outcome.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Where errors enter the survey process
text:
Where errors enter the survey process




Note: A larger sample primarily reduces sampling error. It does not correct coverage nonresponse or measurement error.


Champ Figure 3.2. Use the river example at every transition. An address frame can omit some households. A random sample differs from the frame by chance. Some sampled households do not respond. A completed answer can still mismeasure the intended preference.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Four types of errors








Error
Question to ask
Possible response




Coverage
Who has no chance of appearing in the frame
Improve or combine frame sources


Sampling
How much does the selected sample vary by chance
Use design-based uncertainty and adequate sample size


Nonresponse
Does response relate to the outcome
Track response and compare observed characteristics


Measurement
Does the answer represent the intended construct
Revise and test the instrument




A larger sample primarily reduces sampling error. It does not correct coverage nonresponse or measurement error.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: A good secondary source may still need supplementation
text:
A good secondary source may still need supplementation
If you can accomplish your research objective using a secondary source, you may still need to merge it with other data.
Before adding another source identify what is missing

A variable needed for the model
Coverage of part of the target population
Observations from a different time or place
Precision for a subgroup

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Adding variables and adding observations differ
text:
Adding variables and adding observations differ







Supplement
What can change




Variables for sampled units
Measurement definitions, match quality, and spatial or temporal scale


Observations from another source
Coverage, recruitment, selection probabilities, weights, and target population

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Does the new source add information to existing units or adds new units to the sample?
text:
Does the new source add information to existing units or adds new units to the sample?

Adding a water-quality measure does not alter the original selection probabilities if all sampled units remain in the analysis.
Dropping unmatched units can make the analysis sample selective.
Appending respondents from an online panel can change the sample design and the population represented.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Combining sources does not create a probability sample
text:
Combining sources does not create a probability sample
Suppose an existing survey represents licensed anglers and an added intercept survey recruits people at river access points
The combined data still exclude

Unlicensed users
Residents who do not visit the river
Households with passive-use values only

The two sources also have different selection mechanisms and may include some people twice
The combined sample may answer a question about recruited river users. It does not represent all county households without additional design information

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Check in

Sampling
Sampling errors
Adding variables vs. adding observations

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Considerations for questionnaire design
The construct “angling experience” could mean skill, years fishing, trip frequency, or equipment use.
The construct must be defined before it can be measured.
For each desired measure specify

The theoretical concept (take this from your conceptual framework)
The observable response needed (what is your outcome)
The question a respondent can understand (this takes trial and error)
The response options or recording rule
The analysis variable and units

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: In a nonmarket valuation study, questionnaires need defined components
text:
In a nonmarket valuation study, questionnaires need defined components
The respondent needs to understand

Baseline conditions without the program
The specific environmental change
How and when the program would be implemented
The payment mechanism amount and duration
The choice the respondent is being asked to make

The description should be accurate neutral and understandable to the study population

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Question-design checks
Before testing a question ask whether it

Measures one defined concept
Uses language familiar to respondents
Provides a clear reference period
Uses response options that match the question
Avoids leading wording and unsupported information
Places recall demands within what respondents can reasonably report

Question order can also affect answers and should be planned and tested

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Exercise: repair the valuation question

Do you agree that our valuable local rivers should receive more funding so families can enjoy cleaner water and better fishing?

Based on this question, what are some issues?

The policy change is undefined
The payment mechanism is missing
Multiple concepts are combined in one question
The words encourage agreement
The respondent has no choice to decide among

What could a revised question look like?

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
One possible revision

Without the program, current river conditions are expected to continue. The county would restore ten miles of river over five years with the stated changes described in the survey. Each county household would pay an annual fee of $X for five years. If the program and fee appeared together on the ballot, would you vote for or against the program?


This is a classroom revision rather than a validated contingent valuation instrument. The environmental outcomes baseline implementation mechanism payment vehicle and consequentiality would require credible supporting detail and testing.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
One possible revision: broken down
Baseline Without the program current river conditions are expected to continue

Program The county would restore ten miles of river over five years with the stated changes described in the survey


Payment Each county household would pay an annual fee of $X for five years


Choice If the program and fee appeared together on the ballot would you vote for or against the program


This is a classroom revision rather than a validated contingent valuation instrument. The environmental outcomes baseline implementation mechanism payment vehicle and consequentiality would require credible supporting detail and testing.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Questions still need to be tested
text:
Questions still need to be tested
Ask potential respondents

What do you think the program would change
What does the payment mean for your household
Which information did you use to decide
Which words were unclear or interpreted differently
What assumptions did you make that were not stated

Cognitive (one-on-one) interviews reveal how respondents understand and answer the question

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Develop test and refine the instrument
text:
Develop test and refine the instrument

Start with a focus group
Draft instrument
Seek expert review
Perform cognitive (one-on-one) interviews

To test:

Revise instrument
Pilot survey
Develop final instrument

Revisions can change the questions, recruitment materials, mode, and field procedures

Champ notes that the final questionnaire may bear little resemblance to the first draft. A pilot also provides information about response rates implementation costs follow-up needs and the distribution of willingness to pay.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Mode changes the data-generating process
Mode = how the survey is administered







Self-administered
Interviewer-administered




Lower cost per response in many settings
Greater control over eligibility order and completion


Privacy and respondent pacing
Ability to clarify a complex instrument


Requires literacy and clear instructions
Requires trained interviewers


Greater risk of unanswered or reordered questions
Greater risk of interviewer and social-desirability effects



Online mail phone and in-person modes also reach different people and can produce different response patterns

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Fieldwork begins before the first response
text:
Fieldwork begins before the first response
A sound primary data collection process requires researchers to prepare a written protocol for

Eligibility and recruitment
Consent and confidentiality
Survey administration and permitted clarification
Follow-up contacts
Tracking responses and field outcomes
Escalating unexpected situations
Protecting identifiers and survey data

Institutional review and data-security requirements should be resolved before collection. Similar best practices when using secondary data.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Train interviewers and enumerators
Training should cover

The study purpose without coaching a preferred response
Standard wording order and neutral probes
Eligibility consent and confidentiality procedures
Practice interviews and feedback
Recording refusals partial interviews and deviations
Procedures for technical or safety problems

Supervisors should confirm that each enumerator can administer the protocol consistently before fieldwork

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Quality assurance during collection

Track invitations contacts completions refusals and ineligible cases
Review early records before collection accelerates
Check ranges skips duplicates timestamps and unusual patterns
Debrief enumerators and document protocol deviations
Preserve the original response before any correction
Compare early and late respondents when useful

Quality checks should identify both data errors and failures in the collection process

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Write the codebook before collection
For every field record

Variable name and label
Exact question or source
Unit and reference period
Allowed values and labels
Codes for missing refused and not applicable
Skip logic
Derived-variable rule
Instrument and codebook version

Writing the codebook early exposes questions that cannot yet be coded consistently

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
section: Zero, missing, refused, and not applicable differ
text:
Zero, missing, refused, and not applicable differ
In your codebook, make note of what is a missing response versus a zero, refused, or N/A.
Consider annual river visits



Recorded value
Meaning




0
Respondent made no visits


NA_DK
Respondent does not know


NA_REF
Respondent refused


NA_SKIP
Question did not apply because of the survey path


blank
Collection or processing status is unresolved



Collapsing these values changes the meaning of the analysis variable

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Documentation supports assessment and reuse
Document while the study is in progress

Study objective and protocol
Population frame and sample selection
Instrument recruitment scripts and contact dates
Pilot changes and instrument versions
Fieldwork training costs and deviations
Codebook cleaning rules and validation checks
Final sample disposition and summary statistics
Raw-data archive access and confidentiality conditions

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Check in
What is one practice you have used or learned from an advisor mentor or field team?

Was this a practice that occurred before, during, or after collection?
Which failure was is intended to prevent?
Could it apply broadly or does it depend on the study context?


Organize contributions on the board under before collection during collection and after collection. Distinguish a documented quality-control procedure from a preference that may be specific to one field setting.

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Apply Champ to your research
For one data source in your project explain

Why primary or secondary data are appropriate
Which population the study is intended to represent
How units enter the observed sample
Which error is the largest threat to inference
How the key measure will be tested or validated
Which fieldwork and documentation record another researcher would need

title: Lecture 5.1: Data Collection: Surveys
text:
Summary
Source choice follows from the research objective and required measure
Sampling determines which population can be represented
Questionnaire design turns concepts into responses that can be interpreted
Fieldwork and processing determine whether the design is implemented consistently
Documentation makes those decisions assessable and reproducible

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Readings and sequence

Ethridge, Chapter 8

What a conceptual framework does in applied economic research

Varian, “How to Build an Economic Model in Your Spare Time”

How to isolate a mechanism and structure a useful model

Romer, “Mathiness in the Theory of Economic Growth”

How to keep verbal mathematical and empirical arguments aligned



This lecture follows the readings in sequence and uses the SNAP project to connect their arguments.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Example: SNAP retailer stocking requirements
SNAP-authorized retailers must satisfy program eligibility standards. Eligibility requires a minimum assortment of staple foods.
In 2018, a new rule went into effect that changed the minimum number of items per food category to remain eligible.
Changes in how qualifying varieties (breadth) and stocking units (depth) are defined may affect

Products carried by participating retailers
Cost of remaining SNAP authorized
Retailer entry into the program and/or continued participation and/or exit
Access to staple foods for SNAP households


Keep the policy description brief. The purpose is to establish the research problem rather than provide the full institutional background.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: The core policy issue and rationale
text:
The core policy issue and rationale
Policy concern
Previous minimum standards could allow SNAP participation with limited nutritious variety

Policy intervention
Require more varieties across staple food categories and more perishable foods


Intended mechanism
Use the value of SNAP authorization to encourage neighborhood retailers to stock more nutritious foods


Longer-run goal
Improve convenient access to foods consistent with dietary guidance in low-income and rural communities


This is the policy rationale. The empirical project evaluates whether the intended mechanism occurs and whether retailer responses alter the result.
The rulemaking record is available through Federal Register docket FNS-2025-0018.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Translating the policy issue into a research problem

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Begin with a researchable problem
Broad policy question

Do stronger stocking standards improve access to staple foods?

Researchable questions

How do revised standards affect continued SNAP authorization?
Which types of retailers are more likely to lose authorization?
How does the portfolio and location of authorized retailers change?
Are authorization losses concentrated in areas with a higher share of SNAP-participating households?


If losses are concentrated where SNAP participation is highest then the policy change may be poorly targeted with respect to retailer access.
This question connects the distribution of retailer losses to the communities the program is intended to serve.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Where does the conceptual framework enter?
text:
Where does the conceptual framework enter?
These parts often develop together while writing a manuscript

The problem statement identifies the possible loss of SNAP-authorized retailers
The literature review offers theory and evidence about regulation retailer participation and food access
The conceptual framework explains why the rule may change authorization and predicts which stores and communities are most affected
The methods use annual store authorization and location data to evaluate those predictions

Distinguish the conceptual framework from the empirical design

The framework states the expected relationships
The empirical design specifies how the evidence will be used to estimate them

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Ethridge: conceptualize the problem
For Ethridge, a conceptual framework is an analysis of a specific research problem using relevant theory and concepts (Ethridge 2004).
The framework applies theory to explain the relationships that create or characterize the problem.
It is not a review of standard theory and it is not a description of the empirical method.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Five elements of a conceptual framework
text:
Five elements of a conceptual framework
Ethridge draws on Williams to describe an organized analysis that may include

Sources of the problem
Proposed solutions to the problem
Variables relevant to the analysis
Relationships organized into a system
Hypotheses about expected results

Source: Ethridge Chapter 8 pages 130–131

This five-item list comes directly from Ethridge’s discussion of Williams. It replaces the earlier six-item checklist which was a synthesis rather than a list stated by Ethridge.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Applying the five elements to the SNAP example
text:
Applying the five elements to the SNAP example
Source of the problem Some SNAP retailers may offer limited nutritious variety

Proposed solution Stronger stocking standards


Relevant variables Authorization status, store type, location, and neighborhood-level SNAP participation rates


Relationship Compliance costs alter the retailer’s decision to remain authorized


Expected result Authorization losses vary across store types and communities

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Three kinds of hypotheses in Ethridge
text:
Three kinds of hypotheses in Ethridge







Type
Role in the conceptual framework




Maintained hypotheses
Assumptions accepted for purposes of the analysis


Diagnostic hypotheses
Proposed explanations for the source or nature of the problem


Remedial hypotheses
Proposed actions expected to address the diagnosed problem



Maintained hypotheses define the conditions for the reasoning. Diagnostic hypotheses explain the problem. Remedial hypotheses connect a proposed intervention to a response.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Apply the three hypothesis types
Maintained hypothesis
Meeting the stronger stocking standard is costly for at least some retailers

Diagnostic hypothesis
Some SNAP households have limited access to nutritious foods because nearby retailers stock too few qualifying products


Remedial hypothesis
A stronger stocking standard increases nutritious inventory among retailers that comply and remain authorized


Stress that maintained hypotheses are analytically distinct from diagnostic and remedial hypotheses. The example statements are starting points that require refinement as the model is developed.
Inventory is the policy mechanism in this example but it is not observed in the proposed empirical application. The observed response is whether a store remains authorized.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: The conceptual framework also identifies competing responses
text:
The conceptual framework also identifies competing responses
The intended policy mechanism is not the only possible response.

Some retailers already meet the new standard
Some retailers change inventory and remain authorized
Some retailers decide that compliance is not worthwhile
Some retailers lose authorization
Authorization losses may be concentrated by store type or community

The framework distinguishes the unobserved stocking mechanism from the observed authorization outcome.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
How Ethridge recommends proceeding

Review how related problems have been conceptualized
Reduce the problem to its simplest useful form
Identify the applicable economic theory
Construct a base model using maintained hypotheses
Add dimensions only when they improve the analysis
Assemble hypotheses from the conceptual reasoning

Source: Ethridge Chapter 8 pages 136–138

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Discussion: apply Ethridge to your research
text:
Discussion: apply Ethridge to your research

What specific condition or relationship requires explanation in your project
Which theory helps you reason through that problem
What maintained hypothesis does your reasoning require
What diagnostic hypothesis follows from the framework
What remedial hypothesis would correspond to a proposed intervention


Students can answer using their own dissertation idea or another current project. The questions do not require knowledge of SNAP policy.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: From the concept to the model
text:
From the concept to the model
Ethridge asks what the conceptual framework must accomplish

Apply relevant theory to the research problem and derive meaningful hypotheses


Varian asks how the economic model should be structured


Identify agents, choices, objectives, constraints, interactions, and adjustment

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Varian: start with the following questions
text:
Varian: start with the following questions

Who makes choices?
What can each agent choose?
What objective guides each choice?
What constraints limit each agent?
How do the agents interact?
What adjusts when choices are not mutually consistent?

Work through the simplest example that retains the mechanism. Add complexity only when it changes the result (Varian 1997).

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Structure the example: agents and choices
text:
Structure the example: agents and choices
Who makes choices and what can they choose?

Retailers decide whether the value of SNAP authorization justifies the cost of meeting the rule


Households choose among the retailers available to them


The regulator sets stocking standards and determines eligibility


Pause after the question and solicit possibilities before revealing each response.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Structure the example: objectives and constraints
text:
Structure the example: objectives and constraints
What do agents want and what limits their choices?

Retailers value SNAP-related revenue and face compliance procurement shelf-space and spoilage costs


Households value food and other goods and face income travel time prices and product availability


The regulator seeks healthier food access and program integrity within administrative constraints


Pause after the question and let students identify objectives and constraints before revealing the example.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Structure the example: interaction and adjustment
text:
Structure the example: interaction and adjustment
How do choices interact and what adjusts?

The stocking standard changes compliance costs for some retailers


The value of SNAP customers affects a retailer’s willingness to incur those costs


Retailers enter remain in or leave the authorized-store network


The number type and location of authorized stores adjust across communities

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
A first model: retailer authorization
Let rr represent the strictness of the stocking standard.

For retailer ii
Bi=value of SNAP authorization
B_i=\text{value of SNAP authorization}

Ki(r)=cost of meeting the stocking standard
K_i(r)=\text{cost of meeting the stocking standard}



The observed authorization outcome is
ai(r)={1if Bi≥Ki(r)0if Bi<Ki(r)
a_i(r)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } B_i\geq K_i(r)\\
0 & \text{if } B_i<K_i(r)
\end{cases}

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: When does the rule force a change?
text:
When does the rule force a change?
Requires a change — binding
The new standard requires a retailer to change its inventory to remain eligible

Already satisfied — slack
The retailer already meets the standard so the rule does not require an inventory change


Inventory without the program minimum — unconstrained inventory
The inventory a retailer would choose without the program minimum. It does not mean that the retailer is exempt from the rule.


Without inventory data the empirical analysis cannot identify which individual stores faced a binding standard. The distinction remains useful as a theoretical explanation for why the policy affects some stores more than others.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Developing a conceptual model
For market or neighborhood mm the number of authorized retailers is
Am(r)=∑i∈mai(r)
A_m(r)=\sum_{i\in m}a_i(r)


The portfolio also describes

The number of authorized stores
The types of stores that remain
Their geographic distribution
The communities that experience losses


Here Am(r)A_m(r) is the number of authorized retailers in market mm under stocking standard rr. The outcome is the authorized-store network rather than the quantity of inventory.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Program targeting
Let SmS_m denote the share of households participating in SNAP in community mm.
If authorization losses are larger where SmS_m is higher then the authorized-store network contracts most in communities that rely more heavily on SNAP.
That pattern would suggest a targeting problem relative to the policy’s food-access goal.
It would not by itself establish the effect on store inventory household purchases diet or health.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: From the model to observable measures
text:
From the model to observable measures







Model object
Empirical counterpart




rr
Implementation of the revised stocking standard


aita_{it}
Store ii authorization status in year tt


AmtA_{mt}
Number and composition of authorized stores in market mm and year tt


SmtS_{mt}
Share of households participating in SNAP



The empirical analysis asks how aita_{it} and AmtA_{mt} changed after the policy and whether those changes vary with SmtS_{mt}.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Maintained hypotheses behind the result

Meeting the new standard is more costly for some retailers than for others
SNAP authorization has positive but heterogeneous value across retailers
Retailers can remain authorized lose authorization or operate outside SNAP
The policy can change the authorized-store portfolio even when inventory is not observed

These maintained hypotheses support the authorization mechanism. They do not establish its empirical magnitude.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Romer: keep words and symbols connected
text:
Romer: keep words and symbols connected
Romer’s concern is not the use of mathematics. It is slippage among

What the verbal argument says
What the mathematical model establishes
What the empirical evidence can support

Mathematical notation improves the argument only when terms are defined consistently and the conclusion follows from the stated assumptions (Romer 2015).

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: What belongs in the written framework?
text:
What belongs in the written framework?
For your project the conceptual framework should state

The problem that requires explanation
The relevant theory and concepts
The agents, choices, objectives, and constraints
The mechanisms connecting the proposed cause to the outcome
The maintained diagnostic and remedial hypotheses
The conditions under which each prediction applies

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
text:
Research-design implications
The framework generates design questions

What is the appropriate unit of analysis
How will loss of authorization be distinguished from store closure
Which store characteristics define the portfolio
Which geography defines the relevant community
How will local SNAP participation be measured
When can each outcome respond
Which adjustments could affect the comparison group

These questions should inform the empirical design.

title: Lecture 4.1: Conceptual Framework and Theory
section: Apply the sequence to your research
text:
Apply the sequence to your research

Problem State the condition that requires explanation
Theory Identify the concepts that help explain it
Structure Identify agents, choices, objectives, constraints, and adjustment
Prediction State what should change and under which conditions
Boundary State what the model does not establish
Evidence Identify an observation that would challenge the proposed mechanism

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Presenting the model in a paper
text:
Presenting the model in a paper
Lecture 4.1 developed a conceptual model of retailer authorization.
The next step is to present that reasoning in a paper

Explain why the theory is relevant to the research problem
Define the agents, choices, program rules, assumptions, and relationships
Show how the prediction follows from the model
Connect the prediction to the available evidence

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Recall the retailer participation model
For retailer ii

BiB_i is the benefit from SNAP authorization including SNAP-related sales
Ki(r)K_i(r) is the cost of meeting stocking standard rr
ai(r)a_i(r) records whether the retailer is authorized

ai(r)=1whenBi≥Ki(r)
a_i(r)=1 \quad \text{when} \quad B_i\geq K_i(r)

A stronger standard may raise Ki(r)K_i(r) by different amounts across retailers. If the cost rises above BiB_i the model predicts a change from authorized to unauthorized.

BiB_i is the benefit the retailer receives from authorization. It may include SNAP-related sales and access to SNAP customers. It is not a government payout. The revised standard applies to authorized retailers generally. The added cost may be zero or small for a store that already meets it and larger for a store that has to change its inventory.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Review the following claim

Because stricter stocking standards require healthier foods, they improve food access and diet quality.

Use the retailer model on the previous slide to assess the claim.

What does the model predict?
The standard may raise compliance costs and cause some retailers to lose authorization which can reduce the number of SNAP outlets in a community


What do the available data observe?
Whether stores remain authorized and how the authorized-store network changes


What requires additional evidence?
Changes in inventory food availability purchases diet and health


The quoted claim describes an intended policy pathway. The retailer participation model adds another pathway through compliance cost and authorization. Ask students to distinguish the model result from the later outcomes that would require separate measures and relationships.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Theory in an empirical paper
Chouinard emphasizes making the theory that motivates the research question and hypotheses explicit (Chouinard 2015).
For an empirical paper the theory section can

Explain the mechanism behind the research question
State the assumptions needed for that mechanism
Derive the hypotheses evaluated with data
Connect theoretical concepts to empirical measures
State the limits of the conclusions supported by the evidence

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: The role of theory depends on the contribution
text:
The role of theory depends on the contribution







Theoretical paper
Empirical paper




Develop or modify a model
Apply theory to explain the empirical question


Establish analytical results
Derive hypotheses and comparative predictions


Show what changes relative to prior theory
Connect concepts to observed measures


Treat the model as a central contribution
Use the model to organize the empirical argument



Both require explicit assumptions and a coherent sequence of reasoning.

section: Varying degrees of theory in a paper
text:
Varying degrees of theory in a paper
Apply established theory
Summarize the relevant result and explain how it applies to the research problem

Modify established theory
State the baseline model, identify the change, and show how the result changes


Develop new theory
Define the setting, assumptions, relationships, and results in sufficient detail to establish the contribution

The appropriate level of detail depends on how theory contributes to the paper.

Chouinard cautions against rederiving familiar theory when the contribution is an application. More detail is warranted when the paper changes the model or contributes new theory.
[Sources] - Chouinard (2015/Sources)

text:
Present the model in a logical order
Chouinard recommends introducing the model components before presenting the complete argument.

Define the setting and relevant agents
Identify choices and institutional constraints
State the maintained assumptions
Introduce the relationships among model objects
Derive and interpret the conditional result

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply the sequence: setting, agents, choices, and constraints
text:
Apply the sequence: setting, agents, choices, and constraints
Setting and agents SNAP-authorized retailers respond to a revised stocking standard

Choice Each retailer decides whether authorization remains worthwhile


Institutional constraint A retailer must satisfy the stocking standard to remain eligible for SNAP authorization

The stocking rule limits the retailer’s feasible choices.
A compliance cost is a consequence of responding to that rule rather than the constraint itself.

Use constraint for a limit on choice imposed by the setting. Here the eligibility rule is the constraint. Do not use constraint as a synonym for an assumption or a cost.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply the sequence: assumptions, relationship, and result
text:
Apply the sequence: assumptions, relationship, and result
Maintained assumptions
These are conditions accepted for the model comparison

The stronger standard does not reduce compliance cost and may raise it by different amounts across retailers
BiB_i is held fixed when comparing the two standards
Retailers compare the benefit of authorization with the cost of compliance


Relationship ai(r)=1a_i(r)=1 when Bi≥Ki(r)B_i\geq K_i(r)


Conditional result Authorization changes when Ki(r)K_i(r) rises from no greater than BiB_i to greater than BiB_i

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Interpret the central terms consistently
For retailer ii

rr is the strictness of the stocking standard
BiB_i is the benefit of authorization including SNAP-related sales
Ki(r)K_i(r) is the cost of meeting standard rr
ai(r)a_i(r) is authorization status

The index ii allows benefits and costs to differ across retailers.

The benefit of authorization is not a direct government payout. It represents the private benefit to the retailer including SNAP-related revenue and access to customers who use SNAP benefits. Chouinard recommends recognizable notation defined without delay and used consistently.
[Sources] - Chouinard (2015/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Pair the equation with its interpretation
text:
Pair the equation with its interpretation
The retailer remains authorized when the benefit of authorization covers the compliance cost
ai(r)={1if Bi≥Ki(r)0if Bi<Ki(r)
a_i(r)=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } B_i\geq K_i(r)\\
0 & \text{if } B_i<K_i(r)
\end{cases}

A change in the standard changes authorization only when compliance cost moves from at or below BiB_i to above BiB_i.

Define the symbols before or immediately after displaying the equation. Then give the economic interpretation. The equation and prose should make the same claim.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Separate the model result from the empirical hypothesis
text:
Separate the model result from the empirical hypothesis
Model result
Holding BiB_i fixed, a higher Ki(r)K_i(r) can cause a retailer to lose authorization

Empirical hypothesis
Retailers expected to face higher compliance costs are more likely to lose authorization after implementation


Evidence
Store-year authorization data can show whether losses differ by observable retailer characteristics

The evidence may support or challenge the hypothesis without revealing the unobserved compliance cost itself.

section: Discussion: apply Chouinard to your research
text:
Discussion: apply Chouinard to your research

What role does theory serve in your paper
Are you applying modifying or developing a model
Which concept must be defined before the reader sees an equation
Which assumption carries your principal result
What empirical hypothesis follows from that result


Use whole-class discussion. Students may answer using a dissertation chapter or another current project. Ask for the relationship among the five answers rather than separate summaries.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Cheng’s structure: premises reasoning and conclusion
text:
Cheng’s structure: premises reasoning and conclusion
Cheng describes a proof as a sequence of statements in which each statement follows from what came before (Cheng 2004).



Part
Function in an economic argument




Beginning
Definitions assumptions and accepted results


Middle
The steps connecting the premises to the result


End
The claim the argument was constructed to establish



The written argument makes the intermediate steps visible.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Develop the argument backward and present it forward
text:
Develop the argument backward and present it forward
When developing an argument it is useful to ask

What would have to be true for this conclusion to follow?


That question works backward from the intended result and helps identify the required assumptions and intermediate steps.


The written argument should then proceed forward from the stated premises to the result.


Cheng distinguishes the order in which a proof may be discovered from the order in which it should be written. The same distinction applies to an economic argument.
[Sources] - Cheng (2004/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Apply Cheng’s structure to the retailer model
text:
Apply Cheng’s structure to the retailer model
Beginning
The revised standard may raise Ki(r)K_i(r) while BiB_i is held fixed

Middle
A retailer remains authorized only when Bi≥Ki(r)B_i\geq K_i(r)


End
For a retailer whose compliance cost rises above the benefit of authorization the model predicts a change from authorized to unauthorized

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
Show the threshold crossing
Suppose the standard changes from r0r_0 to r1r_1 and
Ki(r0)≤Bi<Ki(r1)
K_i(r_0)\leq B_i<K_i(r_1)

Then
ai(r0)=1andai(r1)=0
a_i(r_0)=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
a_i(r_1)=0

The retailer was authorized under the earlier standard and is not authorized under the stronger standard.

This is a conditional model result. It does not establish that the cost increase occurred or caused an observed authorization loss in the data.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
“Handwaving”
Handwaving is a term that describes a step that may be plausible but is not established by the stated argument
The authorization model can support
higher compliance cost→possible authorization loss
\text{higher compliance cost}
\rightarrow
\text{possible authorization loss}

It does not by itself establish
authorization loss→food access change→diet or health change
\text{authorization loss}
\rightarrow
\text{food access change}
\rightarrow
\text{diet or health change}

That downstream pathway requires relationships and evidence about inventory availability purchases and health.

Handwaving does not mean the conclusion is impossible. It means that the premises and intermediate steps presented so far do not establish it. In this example the omitted steps include whether households used an affected retailer whether alternative retailers replace that access and whether purchases respond.
[Sources] - Cheng (2004/Sources)

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: Two claims that require more support
text:
Two claims that require more support
Invalid converse

A retailer remained authorized therefore the revised requirement was slack

The retailer may instead have changed its inventory to comply.

Unsupported causal attribution

A retailer lost authorization after implementation therefore the revised rule caused the loss

The analysis needs to distinguish policy exposure from closure, reclassification, and other changes over time.

What observed result would be consistent with the conclusion

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
section: SNAP example: hypothesis, evidence, and audit
text:
SNAP example: hypothesis, evidence, and audit
Empirical hypothesis
Authorization losses increase after implementation among retailers expected to face larger compliance-cost increases
Observable evidence
Store-year data show authorization changes by retailer type, location, and local SNAP participation
Takeaways
The argument establishes a conditional prediction about authorization
Changes in inventory, household food access, purchases, diet, or health require additional relationships and evidence

These three slides provide an example of a complete workshop submission. Together they define the problem, agent, choice, constraint, maintained assumptions, result, empirical hypothesis, available evidence, and boundary. Emphasize that the boundary identifies a missing part of the argument rather than declaring the downstream outcomes impossible.

title: Lecture 4.2: Writing the Conceptual Framework
text:
SNAP example: in paragraph form

The revised standard may raise the cost of continued SNAP authorization, with the increase varying across retailers. Let BiB_i denote the benefit a retailer receives from authorization, including SNAP-related sales, and let Ki(r)K_i(r) denote the compliance cost. Holding BiB_i fixed, the model predicts an authorization loss when Ki(r)K_i(r) exceeds BiB_i. This prediction motivates an analysis of authorization changes by store type and local SNAP participation. The available data do not establish changes in inventory, household access, purchases, diet, or health.

Step
What happens
Streamflow example

Source documentation defines the population, measures, timing, geography, and uncertainty

section: Make the project understandable to others
text:
Make the project understandable to others
A collaborator needs to know:

What identifies an observation.
What each transformation does.
How tasks and changes are coordinated.
How to reproduce the result.

Version control supports this work; it does not replace a clear design.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Keys define the observations
A key is a field or combination of fields that uniquely identifies a row








Data structure
One row represents
Possible key




Household survey
One household in one wave
household_id, wave


County panel
One county in one year
county_fips, year


Parcel transactions
One recorded sale
transaction_id



Cleaned tables should have keys that are unique and nonmissing
Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 5

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Check the key before joining
stopifnot(!anyNA(data[c("county_id", "year")]))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(data[c("county_id", "year")]))
Before merging:

State the expected matching relationship.
Inspect unmatched keys.
Compare row counts before and after.

Keep identifiers as text when leading zeros matter.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Exercise: find the merge problem
A county-year table is joined to a county-industry-year table using county and year.

Should the row count increase?
What becomes the unit of observation?
What happens if county population is later summed?
How would you prevent double counting?

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Abstraction: write the idea once
Use a function or loop for repeated transformations.
rate_per_1000 <- function(events, population) {
  stopifnot(all(population > 0))
  1000 * events / population
}
State assumptions about missing values, units, and valid inputs.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Discussion: when does abstraction help?

When is a function clearer than repeated code?
When does a general solution become harder to understand?
What would make a function easier to check?
Which repeated step in your project is worth simplifying?

Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 6.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Documentation explains decisions
Use names and structure to show what code does.
Use comments for:

Why a choice was made.
A source or definition.
An unexpected but intentional rule.
A limitation a future user might miss.

A codebook should define units and missing-value conventions.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
A task needs an owner
A useful task record contains:

A concrete deliverable.
One responsible person.
Inputs and dependencies.
A definition of completion.
A place to record decisions.

What goes wrong in the reading’s email exchange about robustness checks?
Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Section 8.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
section: A branch for a focused change
text:
A branch for a focused change
In the practice repository:
git switch -c clarify-codebook
# Edit the README, then:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Clarify missing-value codes"
git switch main
git merge clarify-codebook
Use the actual default branch name if it is not main.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
A conflict requires a decision

Read both versions and understand their intentions.
Edit the file to the agreed result.
Remove conflict markers.
Check the result, stage it, and complete the merge.

Do not choose a version solely because it is newer.

title: Lecture 5.4: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git II
text:
Code style supports review

Give scripts and functions one clear purpose
Use names that identify the concept and unit
Make function inputs and outputs explicit
Separate key calculations from setup code
Write logical conditions in the form a reader would describe them
Use consistent naming and indentation across the project
Return informative errors for invalid inputs

Source: Gentzkow and Shapiro (2014), Code Style appendix

The key in one dataset.

Where a variable is defined.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Start with four questions

What relationship are you trying to learn about?
What would the ideal experiment look like?
What identification strategy is feasible?
How will you quantify uncertainty?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural and reduced-form approaches







Structural
Reduced-form / design-based




Specifies behavioral relationships
Focuses on variation identifying an effect


Recovers parameters within a model
Often targets a treatment or policy effect


Can support model-based counterfactuals
Often speaks most directly to the studied setting



Both require assumptions. Their usefulness depends on the question.
Source: Timmins and Schlenker (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What a structural model adds

Agents, objectives, constraints, and interactions.
Parameters with a behavioral interpretation.
A way to trace feedback and equilibrium responses.
A framework for welfare or unobserved policy counterfactuals.

Identification still requires informative data and defensible restrictions.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: vehicle policy
The source slides use fuel-economy regulation versus fuel taxation.
A model may need:

Firms’ new-vehicle decisions.
Household vehicle choice and driving.
Used-vehicle markets and scrappage.
Interactions across these decisions.

Which effects would a simple comparison of new-car fuel economy miss?

Adapted from Unit 6, slides 6–8 and the discussion of Jacobsen in Timmins and Schlenker. Focus on the mechanism rather than presenting uncited numerical results.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Structural tradeoffs
Potential gains: explicit mechanisms, feedbacks, welfare analysis, counterfactual simulation.
Challenges: specification, computational demands, identification, and sensitivity to behavioral assumptions.
A counterfactual prediction is conditional on the model remaining appropriate.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What reduced-form designs emphasize

A clearly defined outcome and treatment.
A credible comparison.
Institutional knowledge about assignment.
Variation that isolates the relationship of interest.

Fixed effects, thresholds, instruments, and random assignment are possible tools, not automatic guarantees.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: Timmins and Schlenker
For your proposed question:

Is the goal an effect in an observed setting or a new policy counterfactual?
Which behavioral responses must be represented?
Which assumptions would each approach require?
Could the approaches provide complementary evidence?

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Outcomes we cannot observe together
Let Yi(1)Y_i(1) be an individual’s outcome under treatment and Yi(0)Y_i(0) under no treatment.
Yi=DiYi(1)+(1−Di)Yi(0)
Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)

We observe only one potential outcome for each individual.
The missing counterfactual is the central problem.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Selection contaminates a raw comparison
E[Y∣D=1]−E[Y∣D=0]=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣D=1]+E[Y(0)∣D=1]−E[Y(0)∣D=0].
\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
&=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid D=1]\\
&\quad+E[Y(0)\mid D=1]-E[Y(0)\mid D=0].
\end{aligned}

The first term is the average treatment effect on the treated. The remaining difference is selection bias.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Example: hospitals and health
People who visit hospitals may have worse health than those who do not.

Does that establish that hospitals worsen health?
What would their health have been without treatment?
Which selection process makes the raw comparison misleading?

Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009).

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
What random assignment gives us
Under random assignment:
D⟂(Y(0),Y(1)).
D\;\perp\;(Y(0),Y(1)).

With consistency and no interference, the population difference in means identifies the average treatment effect.
Randomization makes groups comparable in expectation; a realized sample can still be imbalanced.

Corrects Unit 6, slide 24: assignment is independent of potential outcomes, not necessarily of the observed outcome. Imperfect compliance and attrition require additional analysis.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
section: Regression does not remove selection by itself
text:
Regression does not remove selection by itself
In a model such as
Yi=α+τDi+Xi′β+εi,Y_i=\alpha+\tau D_i+X_i'\beta+\varepsilon_i,
a causal interpretation of τ\tau needs assumptions about treatment assignment and the error term.
Controls can help with comparability or precision. They can also introduce problems if chosen without a causal argument.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Read the experimental table



Table from Mostly Harmless Econometrics comparing estimated small-class effects across specifications with additional controls.


Source: Angrist and Pischke; retained from Unit 6, slide 26.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Discussion: what changes across columns?

Which coefficients are stable?
What happens to standard errors?
How can controls improve precision in an experiment?
What would a large change in the treatment coefficient prompt you to investigate?

Start with the table’s sample, units, and assignment process.

title: Lecture 6.1: Econometric Models and Identification
text:
Omitted-variable bias
Suppose the population model is
Y=α+βX+γZ+u,Y=\alpha+\beta X+\gamma Z+u,
but we omit ZZ. Under the usual exogeneity conditions,
plim⁡β̂short=β+γCov⁡(X,Z)Var⁡(X).
\operatorname{plim}\hat\beta_{\text{short}}
=\beta+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.

Both the outcome relevance of ZZ and its association with XX matter.

text:

What alternative explanation remains?

text:
Can you describe the ideal experiment?
Specify treatment, population, assignment, outcome, and follow-up period.
If the treatment itself is ambiguous, refine the question first.

Preserves the source speaker-note example: changing school-start age may also change schooling duration or age at testing. Ask students which effect their hypothetical experiment would isolate.

Before class

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Begin with the task
Are we trying to:

Predict an outcome?
Describe patterns?
Estimate a causal effect?
Learn how effects vary?

The task determines how success should be evaluated.
Source: Athey and Imbens (2019).

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Prediction and causality
A model can predict outcomes well using variables that do not cause them.
A causal question asks how outcomes change under an intervention.
Predictive accuracy alone does not justify changing a policy variable.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Supervised and unsupervised learning

Supervised: learn a relationship between inputs and observed outcomes.
Unsupervised: find structure without an outcome label.

Examples: predicting demand versus grouping similar observations.
Both can contribute to economic research when the role is explicit.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Overfitting
A flexible model can fit noise in its training sample.

Evaluate performance on observations not used to fit the model.
Keep the final test set separate from model selection.
Respect the dependence structure when splitting data.

For forecasting, information from the future should not enter training.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Bias and variance
Greater flexibility may reduce approximation bias while increasing variability.
Regularization constrains the fit to improve performance outside the training sample.
The best training fit is not necessarily the best predictive model.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
LASSO
A common form minimizes
1n∑i=1n(Yi−α−Xi′β)2+λ∑j=1p|βj|.
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\alpha-X_i'\beta)^2
+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|.


The penalty shrinks coefficients and may set some to zero.
The tuning parameter controls the penalty.
Cross-validation can guide predictive tuning.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Trees and forests
A regression tree splits observations into groups with different predicted outcomes.
A random forest averages predictions across many randomized trees.



Illustrative regression tree with splitting rules and terminal-node predictions, retained from the source deck.


Source: Unit 6, slide 43.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Exercise: identify leakage
A model predicts whether a household will miss a payment.
One input is “number of collection calls made during the following month.”

Why might this variable predict well?
Could it be known at prediction time?
How would you redesign the evaluation?

This is a hypothetical example.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:
Model selection and confounding
Selecting variables only for predicting the outcome can omit variables important for treatment assignment.
The reading discusses selecting predictors of both outcome and treatment, then using their union in an appropriate estimation procedure.
This still depends on the underlying identification assumptions.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
section: Machine learning within a causal design
text:
Machine learning within a causal design
Flexible methods may estimate nuisance relationships such as:

Expected outcomes conditional on covariates.
Treatment probabilities.

Sample splitting and specialized inference can help manage overfitting.
Machine learning does not supply exogenous variation by itself.

title: Lecture 6.3: Machine Learning in Economic Research
text:

Where can prediction tools improve an economic research workflow?
Why is ordinary predictive validation insufficient for a causal claim?
What is the difference between selecting controls and identifying treatment effects?
Which example in the reading would be useful for your project?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Before class

Gibson, “Are You Estimating the Right Thing? An Editor Reflects” (Gibson 2019).
