title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Credibility involves more than identification
A strong design can still estimate a quantity different from the one the researcher intends.
Check:

Research question.
Estimand.
Measurement.
Population.
Interpretation.

Source: Gibson (2019).

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Does the measure match the concept?
text:
Does the measure match the concept?

Does a registry describe residents or registered persons?
Does expenditure reflect quantity, quality, or both?
Does infrequent recall obscure variation within a period?
Does aggregation hide the response of interest?

Institutional knowledge of the data matters.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Avoid discarding information unnecessarily
A continuous measure can be converted into an indicator, but that discards information.
Example: income versus an indicator for income below a poverty threshold.
Explain why the indicator matches the question. Consider how measurement error near the cutoff changes classification.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Spatial processes cross boundaries
A policy in one area may affect neighbors.

Does the outcome depend on nearby exposure?
Could the comparison group be affected?
Does the estimated effect include spillovers?
Does aggregation hide them?

Match the model and interpretation to the spatial process.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: Gibson

Which example most clearly separates the intended and estimated quantity?
Where does the problem enter: measurement, sample, design, or interpretation?
Would a larger dataset solve it?
Where would your project benefit most from additional effort?


The source notes raise critiques of design-focused research. Treat them as questions about research priorities, not as a claim that all experimental designs require the same assumptions as all structural models.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Statistical significance answers a limited question
text:
Statistical significance answers a limited question
A p-value is the probability, under the null model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic.
It is not:

The probability that the null is true.
The probability that the result will replicate.
The economic importance of the effect.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Type I error, Type II error, and power
text:
Type I error, Type II error, and power



Decision
Null true
Specified alternative true




Reject null
Type I error
Correct rejection


Do not reject
Correct non-rejection
Type II error




α\alpha: probability of Type I error.
β\beta: probability of Type II error under a specified alternative.
Power: 1−β1-\beta.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Sample size changes power



Two panels from Kim showing null and alternative test-statistic distributions and different power as sample size changes.


Source: Kim; retained from Unit 6, slide 71.
With a valid fixed-level test, increasing sample size does not inherently increase the nominal Type I error rate.

Corrects the original large-sample discussion. Larger samples increase power against fixed alternatives. Misspecification, multiple testing, or interpreting tiny effects as important are separate problems.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Statistical and economic importance
A very small effect may be precisely estimated.
Ask:

What is the estimate in meaningful units?
What range is compatible with the data and assumptions?
What effect would matter for the decision?
Could the result be a precise estimate of a biased quantity?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: Kim’s diagnosis

Why does Kim object to relying on a single significance threshold?
Which concerns involve sample size, measurement, or model misspecification?
Which involve repeated testing or selective reporting?
What would a useful statistical toolbox add?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Large samples do not erase bias
text:
Large samples do not erase bias
More observations can reduce variance while leaving systematic error.
MSE⁡(θ̂)=Var⁡(θ̂)+Bias⁡(θ̂)2.
\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta)
=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)
+\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)^2.

Precision can make a biased estimate look convincing.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Bayesian evidence asks another question
A Bayes factor compares the marginal likelihood of the data under two models.
Posterior odds equal prior odds times the Bayes factor.
Neither a Bayes factor nor a posterior probability is the same as a p-value. State the hypotheses and prior assumptions.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Error costs and decision thresholds
An illustrative expected-loss criterion is
L=π0CIα+(1−π0)CIIβ,
L=\pi_0 C_I\alpha+(1-\pi_0)C_{II}\beta,

where π0\pi_0 is the prior probability of the null and CI,CIIC_I,C_{II} are the costs of the two errors.
Choosing a threshold involves the decision context and the test’s operating characteristics.
Source: discussion in Kim (2019).

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
section: Equivalence is not failure to reject
text:
Equivalence is not failure to reject
A nonsignificant test against zero does not establish that the effect is negligible.
Equivalence testing instead specifies a substantively meaningful interval (−Δ,Δ)(-\Delta,\Delta).
The question is whether evidence supports the effect lying inside that interval.
Choose Δ\Delta using the economic question.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Exercise: interpret two findings
Hypothetical findings:

Study A: estimated effect 0.010.01, interval [0.009,0.011][0.009,0.011].
Study B: estimated effect 1.01.0, interval [−0.2,2.2][-0.2,2.2].

What can you say about precision, compatibility with zero, and economic importance?
What units and decision context are missing?

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
A transparent methods section
Report:

Model and target parameter.
Sample and variable construction.
Source of identifying variation.
Controls and their justification.
Inference procedure.
Planned sensitivity analyses.

Source: Unit 6, slides 85–89.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Discussion: use both readings
A paper reports a small p-value from a large administrative dataset.
Give one question from Gibson and one from Kim that you would ask before accepting the conclusion.
Explain why each question concerns a different part of the argument.

title: Lecture 6.5: Evaluating Empirical Evidence
text:
Workshop: an evidence audit
For your proposal:

State the estimand in words.
Check whether the measure matches it.
Identify the largest source of systematic error.
Define an economically meaningful effect.

Read the decision before drafting a response

What did the editor decide?
Which concerns are central?
What revision is invited or required?
What deadline and submission instructions apply?

A revision invitation is an opportunity, not a guarantee of acceptance.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers

What rejection can teach us
Possible problems include:

Unclear contribution.
A gap between evidence and claims.
Weak organization or exposition.
Poor fit with the journal.
A substantive methodological flaw.

Separate presentation problems from problems requiring new analysis.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:

The reading approaches publication from editors’ and referees’ perspectives.

What makes a contribution recognizable?
How can weak communication obscure useful research?
Which concerns can be addressed through writing?
Which require changing the research itself?

Find an example in the reading for each kind of revision.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers

Choi: persist and listen

Read the criticism carefully.
Look for useful information even in an unwelcome report.
Treat misunderstanding as a reason to improve clarity.
Respond to substance without attacking the reviewer.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Answer each comment directly
For every substantive comment:

State the concern.
Explain your response.
Describe the change or provide a reasoned disagreement.
Identify where the manuscript changed.
State any remaining limitation.

Make the reviewer able to verify your answer.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you agree

We agree that the outcome definition was ambiguous. We now specify the reference period and units in the Data section and use the same definition in Table 1.

Why is this more useful than “Fixed” or “Thank you”?
Hypothetical response example.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
When you disagree

Restate the concern fairly.
Explain why the requested change would not resolve it or would change the question.
Supply evidence or reasoning.
Clarify the manuscript where misunderstanding is plausible.
Acknowledge what remains unresolved.

Disagreement should be specific and verifiable.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: Choi’s recommendations

Which recommendations improve the substance of a revision?
Which concern tone and persistence?
Which advice is context-dependent?
How would you respond if two reviewers made incompatible requests?

Distinguish general advice from a particular editor’s instructions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Fryer: map the response
The response organizes the debate around:

What the analysis claims about racial differences and discrimination.
Selection into police-civilian interactions.
The reliability of police narratives.

Identify where the author agrees, disagrees, or clarifies the scope of a claim.
Source: Fryer (2020).

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:
Discussion: evaluate the response
Choose one of those three issues.

What criticism is being answered?
What evidence or reasoning is offered?
Does the response change the analysis, narrow the claim, or defend the original approach?
What question would you still want answered?

Read this as an exercise in evaluating argument, not as evidence that the underlying debate is settled.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers
text:

Tell the editor and reviewers about important changes beyond their requests:

New data.
A different specification.
Additional checks.
Revised interpretation.

Explain why the change was made and how it affects the conclusions.

title: Lecture 7.2: Responding to Reviewers

The source deck raises transparency in peer review.
Discuss possible effects on:

Accountability and learning.
Candor.
Confidentiality.
Willingness to review.

What publication policy would balance these concerns?

Before using the land-use data
Questions to answer from the CDL documentation

How does the CDL define each crop class, and did the definitions change across years?
How accurate is the classification for this crop and state? (NASS publishes accuracy tables by state)
What do the 30-meter pixels and the map projection imply for small fields?
How are double-cropped fields classified?
Does the study boundary stay the same across years?

The CDL records modeled land-cover classes. Parcel ownership, zoning, and management practices require additional sources

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the streamflow series
Questions to answer from the USGS record

Is this the right monitoring location and parameter (00060, discharge)?
What unit does the series use (cubic feet per second)?
Which values are provisional or revised? In the 2024 download, 72 of 183 days carry the qualifier REVISED
Are any dates missing?
Do reservoirs, diversions, or return flows upstream affect the gauge?
How does one gauge relate to the study area?

The gauge measures conditions at one point on a river network. A study of irrigation access may also require diversion service areas, water rights, or delivery records

Use the read_waterdata functions for the current USGS Water Data APIs. USGS plans to decommission the services used by readNWIS functions in 2027.

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the weather data
Questions to answer from the POWER documentation

How large is the grid cell? (About 0.5° by 0.625°, roughly 55 by 53 km near Fort Collins)
Which coordinates represent each farm, county, or market in the study?
How is each variable defined, and in what unit?
Which time standard defines a day? (POWER daily values use local solar time)
Which data version was retrieved, and can values be revised?

Every location in a grid cell receives the same values, so conditions at individual fields can differ from the cell estimate

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
Before using the ACS estimates
Questions to answer from the ACS documentation

The 2024 five-year estimate pools responses from 2020 to 2024. Does a pooled period suit the question?
How large is each margin of error relative to its estimate?
Which tracts have estimates too uncertain to use?
Are geographic identifiers stored as text, so leading zeros survive?
Which tract boundaries apply? (2020 boundaries for the 2024 release)
Are dollar values adjusted to a common year when comparing periods?

ACS data describe the population and socioeconomic setting; exposure measures come from other sources

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: Example: a JSON response becomes a data frame
text:
Example: a JSON response becomes a data frame
The USGS service returns text like this for each day (simplified)
{"time": "2024-07-01", "value": 86.4, "unit_of_measure": "ft^3/s", "approval_status": "Approved"}
dataRetrieval reads the JSON and turns the records into rows of a data frame
  time       value unit_of_measure approval_status
  2024-07-01  86.4 ft^3/s          Approved
  2024-07-02 162   ft^3/s          Approved
You then work with the data frame; the JSON is never saved unless you save it

The response header names the format in Content-Type: application/json, text/csv, image/tiff, application/x-netcdf

The packages in today’s examples choose a format for you. nasapower, for example, requests CSV

section: Extension: the weather data as a NetCDF grid
text:
Extension: the weather data as a NetCDF grid
Question
How did maximum temperature vary across northern Colorado during the July 2024 heat wave?
Why a different request
The point request returns one grid cell. A regional request returns every cell in a box, over every day requested, in one NetCDF file
Request
NASA POWER, daily maximum temperature, 39.5 to 41.5 N and 104.5 to 106.5 W, July 10 to 16, 2024

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
section: With an API: one request in a script
text:
With an API: one request in a script
library(httr2)
library(terra)

request("https://power.larc.nasa.gov/api/temporal/daily/regional") |>
  req_url_query(parameters = "T2M_MAX", community = "AG",
                `latitude-min` = 39.5, `latitude-max` = 41.5,
                `longitude-min` = -106.5, `longitude-max` = -104.5,
                start = "20240710", end = "20240716", format = "NETCDF") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/raw/power_tmax_2024-07.nc")

tmax <- rast("data/raw/power_tmax_2024-07.nc")
tmax   # 15 grid cells (5 rows x 3 columns), 7 daily layers, degrees C
Each argument replaces a click. The file is saved exactly as the server sent it

title: Lecture 5.2: Data Collection via APIs
text:
What the NetCDF file holds





Three dimensions: longitude, latitude, and day
15 cells x 7 days = 105 values in one 21 KB file
Units (degrees C) and variable names travel inside the file
terra reads each day as one layer of a raster

Fort Collins sits in one of the two hottest cells on July 12. The cells to its west, over the mountains, ran 8 to 9 degrees cooler

title: Lecture 5.3: Managing Data for Reproducibility: Git I
text:
What version control adds
Version control gives a project a documented history. At selected points, it records the state of the project’s files together with the author, date, and reason for the change.
That history allows a researcher to compare versions, recover earlier work, and identify the exact project state used for an analysis or manuscript.
Source: Bryan (2017)

Branches move while tags stay fixed









Branch
Tag




What it identifies
The current commit in an ongoing line of work
One selected commit

The tag remains with the selected commit

Marking a release, data freeze, or submitted version



A tag such as v1.0 gives one commit a durable name that is easier to recognize than its commit hash

Git permits a tag to be deleted and recreated, but the usual practice is to treat a published tag as fixed. A tag does not create a separate line of development. To continue developing from a tagged commit, create a branch from that tag.

A conflict occurs when the branches being combined changed the same part of a file in different ways

Methods (this unit) explains how to turn the conceptual model into an equation with estimable parameters, and why the data identify them
A referee should be able to judge the design before seeing a result


This slide places the section in the paper. The rest of the lecture follows the order of the section itself: the estimation strategy (equation, estimator, inference), then the identification strategy (assumption, threats, robustness), then one research question answered three ways.

section: Bellemare splits the section into what you estimate and why it identifies a causal effect
text:
Bellemare splits the section into what you estimate and why it identifies a causal effect
Estimation strategy
The equations, the estimator, and how inference is done
Identification strategy
The feature of the data that supports a causal interpretation, and what threatens it
Use these as the two parts of your section (Bellemare 2020).

This is the structure from the Bellemare reading in Lecture 2.3, Section 5. His Section 5.1 covers the equation, the estimator, hypothesis tests, and standard errors. Section 5.2 covers identification and the threats to it.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Answer four questions before you write the section
text:
Answer four questions before you write the section







Angrist and Pischke ask
The section reports




What is the causal relationship of interest?
The parameter of interest


What experiment would ideally capture it?
The estimand


What is your identification strategy?
The identifying assumption and the variation


What is your mode of statistical inference?
The population, the sample, and the standard errors



Source: Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1.

Angrist and Pischke call these the four research FAQs. Ask: which of the four is hardest to answer for your proposal right now? Most students will say the second or third.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The ideal experiment tells you which parameter you are after
text:
The ideal experiment tells you which parameter you are after
Question: How will climate change affect US agriculture?

Ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades
Farmers would change crops, irrigation, and planting dates
The target is a long-run effect that includes adaptation
A single hot year is a different experiment with a different answer


Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two estimands that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather.
Ask: in your proposal, what would you randomize, and how long would you wait to measure the outcome?

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The identifying assumption says which comparison is free of selection
text:
The identifying assumption says which comparison is free of selection

A raw comparison mixes the effect with differences that existed anyway
Jurajda treats identification as a search for variation unrelated to those differences
The variation can come from across places, within a place over time, a threshold, or assignment
Write the assumption in one plain sentence, with no notation


Angrist and Pischke, Chapter 2: the observed difference in means equals the average effect on the treated plus selection bias, the difference in untreated outcomes between the two groups. Jurajda’s Example 1.1 makes the same point with veterans’ earnings: are veterans earning more because of service, or are high earners more likely to enlist?
Students do not need the decomposition in their paper. They need the sentence that says why selection bias is zero for the comparison they use.

Open the methods map in a new tab

This is the only slide that shows the methods map. Students should use it as a reference while writing, not as content to memorize. The next six slides walk through the three paths: same question, different variation, different assumption, different estimand.
Timmins and Schlenker frame the tradeoff: a cross-section uses differences in long-term averages that units have adapted to, while a panel uses period-to-period variation and so measures a short-run response.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The Ricardian model compares farmland values across counties with different climates
text:
The Ricardian model compares farmland values across counties with different climates
Vc=α+f(Tc,Pc)+Xc′γ+εc
V_c = \alpha + f(T_c, P_c) + X_c'\gamma + \varepsilon_c


VcV_c: farmland value per acre in county cc
Tc,PcT_c, P_c: long-run average temperature and precipitation
f(⋅)f(\cdot): a quadratic in temperature and precipitation; its slope in TcT_c is the parameter of interest
XcX_c: soil quality and other county characteristics

1. Relationship of interest: the long-run effect of climate on land values, including adaptation (Mendelsohn et al. 1994)

The logic: land markets capitalize the expected profit from farming in a given climate, so land values already reflect how farmers have adapted.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Irrigation shows what a violated Ricardian assumption looks like
text:
Irrigation shows what a violated Ricardian assumption looks like

Irrigated farms draw water from outside the county, so local rainfall matters less
Irrigation is concentrated in drier, hotter counties and raises land values
Pooling irrigated and dryland counties omits a variable correlated with climate
Schlenker, Hanemann, and Fisher re-estimate the model for dryland counties (Schlenker et al. 2005)

Discussion: Which variable in your proposal could play the role of irrigation?

This is a clean example of Bellemare’s “unobserved heterogeneity” threat and of a design response: change the sample so the omitted factor no longer varies.
Expect answers such as access to markets, local policy, or management practices that vary across space with the treatment.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The panel model compares each county with itself in hotter and cooler years
text:
The panel model compares each county with itself in hotter and cooler years
yct=g(Wct)+γc+δt+εct
y_{ct} = g(W_{ct}) + \gamma_c + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{ct}


ycty_{ct}: log crop yield or farm profit in county cc, year tt
WctW_{ct}: growing-season weather, such as degree days and precipitation
g(⋅)g(\cdot): the weather–outcome relationship; its slope is the parameter of interest
γc\gamma_c: county effects; δt\delta_t: year effects

Identifying assumption: within a county, year-to-year deviations in weather are as good as random (Deschênes and Greenstone 2007; Schlenker and Roberts 2009).

Deschênes and Greenstone use farm profits; Schlenker and Roberts use yields and allow temperature effects to be nonlinear. Both rely on the same variation.
Ask: why is weather a more believable source of variation than climate? Farmers cannot choose it, and it is hard to forecast at planting.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Fixed effects make the comparison more credible and change the estimand to a short-run response
text:
Fixed effects make the comparison more credible and change the estimand to a short-run response

County effects remove everything fixed about a county, including soils and its long-run climate
What remains is year-to-year deviation in weather
Farmers cannot fully adapt to one hot year
So the estimate is a short-run response, not the long-run effect of climate

Timmins and Schlenker: the long-run effect can be larger or smaller than the short-run effect (Timmins and Schlenker 2009).

Timmins and Schlenker give both directions. Long-run responses face fewer constraints, so long-run damages can be smaller (Le Chatelier principle). But some short-run responses cannot be sustained; their example is groundwater pumping during a drought, which works for one dry year and not for a permanently drier climate.
The point for the paper: a credibility gain is also a change in what you estimate. The section has to say which one you estimate.

section: Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades
text:
Long differences compare slow changes in climate over decades
Δy‾c=αs+βΔW‾c+Δε‾c
\Delta \bar{y}_c = \alpha_s + \beta\, \Delta \bar{W}_c + \Delta \bar{\varepsilon}_c


Δy‾c\Delta \bar{y}_c: change in county cc’s multi-year average outcome between two periods
ΔW‾c\Delta \bar{W}_c: change in its multi-year average weather over the same periods
αs\alpha_s: state fixed effects; β\beta: the parameter of interest

1. Relationship of interest: the response to gradual climate change, including adaptation (Burke and Emerick 2016)

Burke and Emerick use recent temperature and precipitation trends.

section: Name each threat and say how the design or a robustness check handles it
text:
Name each threat and say how the design or a robustness check handles it







Threat
In the panel weather model




Reverse causality
Farm output does not change the weather


Unobserved heterogeneity
County effects absorb fixed differences; year effects absorb national shocks


Measurement error
Gridded weather misses farm conditions; check a second weather data set


Spillovers
Year effects absorb national price changes, so the estimate excludes them



This is question 5 in detail. Each row needs an answer: the threat does not apply, the design handles it, or a robustness check tests it.

The four threats are Bellemare’s list (Section 5.2): reverse causality, unobserved heterogeneity, measurement error, and spillovers. Dalheimer and Bellemare’s Section 2.2 (shown earlier) walks through the first three in this order.
Classical measurement error in weather attenuates the estimate toward zero.
The record on this design shows why data checks matter: Fisher, Hanemann, Roberts, and Schlenker (2012) identified errors in the weather and climate data used by Deschênes and Greenstone, and Deschênes and Greenstone (2012) replied with corrected estimates.

Latin letters for variables, Greek letters for parameters

Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1.

Bellemare also asks for the estimator by name (OLS, linear probability model, probit, maximum likelihood) and for the standard errors to say what they are robust to. “Robust standard errors” is not enough; “robust to heteroskedasticity” is.

section: Four terms come up in every empirical strategy section
text:
Four terms come up in every empirical strategy section

Parameter of interest: the coefficient that answers your research question
Estimator: the rule that turns data into an estimate of that parameter, such as OLS, maximum likelihood, or a difference in means
Identifying assumption: the condition under which the parameter you estimate equals the relationship you want to learn about
Inference: how you measure the uncertainty in the estimate, through standard errors, clustering, and hypothesis tests


Students often use “estimator” and “identification” interchangeably. They are separate choices. The same identifying assumption can be paired with different estimators, and a correct estimator cannot fix a comparison that is not identified.
Ask: which of the four is hardest to write down for your proposal right now?

What is your identification strategy?
The identifying assumption and the variation behind it


How will you measure uncertainty?
The standard errors, the clustering level, and why



Adapted from Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1.

Angrist and Pischke ask “What is the causal relationship of interest?” Not every paper estimates a causal relationship. A descriptive paper or a forecasting paper still needs an estimating equation; it states what the parameter describes and does not claim more. That is why the causal question is separate here.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The identifying assumption says why the groups you compare are comparable
text:
The identifying assumption says why the groups you compare are comparable

Comparing treated and untreated units measures the treatment effect plus any difference that existed between the groups before treatment
Jurajda’s example: veterans may earn more because of military service, or because people with higher earnings potential were more likely to enlist
That pre-existing difference is selection bias
The identifying assumption states why selection bias is zero for your comparison
Write it in one sentence, without notation


Angrist and Pischke, Chapter 2, write this as a decomposition: the observed difference in means equals the average effect on the treated plus selection bias, the difference in untreated outcomes between the two groups. Students do not need the decomposition in their paper. They need the sentence that explains why the untreated outcomes of the two groups would have been the same.
Jurajda’s notes describe identification as a search for variation that is unrelated to these pre-existing differences.

text:
The ideal experiment tells you which effect you are after
Question: How will a warmer climate affect U.S. agriculture?

Ideal experiment: give some counties a permanently warmer climate, then wait decades
Farmers would change crops, irrigation, and planting dates
The target is a long-run effect that includes this adaptation
A single hot year is a different experiment with a different answer


Angrist and Pischke argue that describing the ideal experiment “helps you formulate causal questions precisely.” Here it separates two effects that are easy to confuse: the effect of climate and the effect of weather.
Ask: in your proposal, what would you randomize, and how long would you wait to measure the outcome?

Identifying assumption: those deviations are as good as random
Relationship estimated: the short-run response to weather, because farmers cannot fully adapt to one hot year
Main threat: short-run responses that would not last under a permanent change

Timmins and Schlenker: the long-run effect can be larger or smaller than the short-run effect (Timmins and Schlenker 2009).

This fills in the panel column. County fixed effects remove everything fixed about a county, including irrigation access and long-run climate. What is left is weather.
Timmins and Schlenker give both directions. Long-run responses face fewer constraints, so long-run damages can be smaller. But some short-run responses cannot be sustained; their example is groundwater pumping, which works for one dry year and not for a permanently drier climate.
The point for the paper: gaining credibility also changed what is estimated, and the section has to say which effect it estimates.

Bellemare calls this section the Empirical Framework, and some papers place it before the data section (Bellemare 2020).

Bellemare’s outline for an applied paper: Introduction, Theoretical Framework, Data and Descriptive Statistics, Empirical Framework, Results and Discussion, Summary and Concluding Remarks. title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A threat to identification biases the estimate; a problem with inference misstates its precision
text:
A threat to identification biases the estimate; a problem with inference misstates its precision

Threat to identification (question 6): the estimate is centered on the wrong value, and a larger sample does not fix it
Problem with inference (question 2): the estimate may be centered correctly, but the standard errors are too small, so confidence intervals are too narrow and tests reject too often
Panel weather example: neighboring counties share weather shocks, so treating their errors as independent overstates precision; cluster at a level that contains that correlation and say why
Either problem leads a referee to doubt the result, so the section addresses both

Source: Bellemare (2020), Sections 5.1 and 5.2.

Students often list clustering as a threat. It is not a threat to identification: clustering does not change the point estimate. It changes how confident we are in it.
Robustness checks can address either problem: alternative samples or controls test the identifying assumption; alternative clustering levels test the inference choice.
We return to inference later in the unit, including how to handle a small number of clusters.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Robustness checks vary your choices; sensitivity analyses relax your assumptions
text:
Robustness checks vary your choices; sensitivity analyses relax your assumptions

Robustness check: re-estimate with another defensible outcome measure, treatment measure, estimator, functional form, or sample, and show the conclusion holds (Bellemare 2020, sec. 6.2)
Sensitivity analysis: ask how far the identifying assumption would have to fail before the conclusion changes, for example how strong an omitted variable would have to be (Athey and Imbens 2017)
Placebo test: estimate an effect that should be zero; Bellemare counts these as robustness checks, and Athey and Imbens list them separately
Why papers include them: researchers try many specifications before choosing one, so readers need evidence that the result was not selected for (Athey and Imbens 2017)

A robustness check asks whether your choices matter. A sensitivity analysis asks how wrong your assumption could be.

Athey and Imbens call these “supplementary analyses”: their purpose is not a better estimate of the main effect but evidence on the credibility of the primary analysis. They cite Leamer on the gap between the single model that classical inference assumes and the many specifications researchers actually try. The sensitivity approaches they discuss include Rosenbaum and Rubin, Imbens, Altonji and coauthors, and Oster.
Bellemare frames robustness checks as a response to higher standards of evidence after the credibility revolution: authors “have to work hard to convince readers that their results were not cherrypicked.”
This is why papers have a robustness section. Each check should name the threat or the choice it tests. Lecture 6.5 returns to this.
Note that “robust” in “robust standard errors” is a different use of the word: those standard errors are robust to a specific feature of the errors, such as heteroskedasticity.

The two are the same idea at different levels: the unit is the description for the reader, and the key is how the computer enforces it. If two rows share the same key, either the key is incomplete or the data contain duplicates, and the estimate will weight some units twice. section: A published paper states the equation, then defines every term
text:
A published paper states the equation, then defines every term



Point out the sequence: the relationship in words, the equation, a definition of every term, then one sentence naming the parameter of interest. The next paragraph explains why they first-difference the equation, which is the estimator choice.
Two small inconsistencies are worth noticing: the text defines pitp_{it} for “county ii” in a country-level paper, and the equation uses e1ite_{1it} while the text defines eite_{it}. Referees catch these, and they are why every term should be defined with the same notation used in the equation.
Footnote 5 in the paper explains why the authors do not cluster standard errors after first-differencing. That is an inference decision stated with a reason.

Bellemare calls this section the Empirical Framework, and some papers place it before the data section (Bellemare 2020).

Bellemare’s outline for an applied paper: Introduction, Theoretical Framework, Data and Descriptive Statistics, Empirical Framework, Results and Discussion, Summary and Concluding Remarks. He notes that the data and empirical sections are often swapped; the Dalheimer and Bellemare paper on the next slides puts the empirical framework first.
Two differences from his outline. He argues that a separate literature review is “almost always entirely unwarranted” in a journal article and recommends a short review of the five to ten closest studies in the introduction; a separate review fits a thesis or dissertation chapter. He recommends a background section when the reader needs institutional detail, such as the provisions of a law.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: A parameter is identified when only one value of it fits the data you could observe
text:
A parameter is identified when only one value of it fits the data you could observe

Imagine an unlimited sample: could you recover the number you want?
If not, the parameter is not identified, and more data or a better estimator will not fix it
Identification depends on assumptions about how the data were generated, not on the sample size
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) draws those assumptions: each arrow is a causal effect, and each missing arrow is an assumption


Bellemare (Section 5.2) uses “identification” in the sense most applied papers now use: causal identification, when a coefficient reflects a causal relationship rather than a partial correlation. He refers to Pearl’s notation for this, the effect of setting a variable rather than observing it.
The next two slides use one question from the readings, the effect of military service on earnings, to show a parameter that is not identified and two ways to identify it.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: When an unobserved factor drives both treatment and outcome, the effect is not identified
text:
When an unobserved factor drives both treatment and outcome, the effect is not identified

A comparison of veterans and nonveterans picks up both the effect and the path through earnings potential. With unlimited data it still cannot separate them (Jurajda 2007, Example 1.1).

Jurajda asks: “Are the (minority) vets earning more because of the military service or are the high-earners more likely to enroll in the army?” The dashed path through earnings potential is selection bias, the term defined in the identification strategy section later today.
The four threats map onto this picture. Unobserved heterogeneity is the dashed node. Reverse causality would be an arrow from earnings back to service. Measurement error means the service box is recorded with error. Spillovers would be an arrow from one person’s service to another person’s earnings.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: The effect becomes identified when you measure the common causes or find variation they do not drive
text:
The effect becomes identified when you measure the common causes or find variation they do not drive

A: Angrist (1998), discussed in Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 3. B: the Vietnam-era draft lottery, Angrist (1990), in Jurajda (2007), Example 3.11.

Panel A is selection on observed characteristics. The military screens applicants on age, schooling, and test scores, so comparing veterans and nonveterans with the same values identifies the effect, if nothing else drives both. Angrist and Pischke note that this is “clearly not guaranteed”: applicants who drop out at the last minute may differ in earnings potential.
Panel B is an instrument. The lottery number changes who serves but is assigned at random, so earnings potential cannot affect it, and it should affect earnings only through service. It identifies the effect for men whose service depended on their lottery number.
The identifying assumption in each panel is the “Requires” line. That is the sentence a paper states in words.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: Six questions organize the section, in the order they appear in a paper
text:
Six questions organize the section, in the order they appear in a paper








Subsection
Question
Where the answer appears




Estimation strategy
1. What is the relationship of interest?
The estimating equation and the parameter of interest



2. How will you measure uncertainty?
The estimator, the standard errors, the clustering level, and why


Identification strategy
3. Is that relationship causal?
Whether the parameter is causal, and if not, what it describes



4. What experiment would ideally measure it?
The effect you are trying to estimate



5. What variation identifies it, and what must be true of that variation?
The identifying assumption



6. What could make the identifying assumption fail?
The threats, and the design choice or robustness check that handles each



Adapted from Angrist and Pischke (2009), Chapter 1, and Bellemare (2020), Section 5.

Angrist and Pischke ask four questions, starting with “What is the causal relationship of interest?” Not every paper estimates a causal relationship. A descriptive paper or a forecasting paper still needs an estimating equation; it states what the parameter describes and does not claim more. That is why question 3 is separate here.
The order follows Bellemare: the estimation strategy (equation, estimator, inference) comes first, then the identification strategy (assumption, threats, robustness). The rest of the lecture follows the same order.

section: The estimation strategy also names the estimator and says how inference is done
text:
The estimation strategy also names the estimator and says how inference is done

The estimator by name, such as OLS, a linear probability model, probit, or maximum likelihood, and why
The hypothesis being tested
What the standard errors are robust to, such as heteroskedasticity; “robust standard errors” alone is not enough
Whether and how standard errors are clustered, at what level, and why
Whether sampling weights are used, and how they were constructed

Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.1. This answers question 2.

The clustering level usually follows the level at which the treatment varies or at which errors are correlated. In the panel weather example later today, neighboring counties share weather shocks.
We return to inference later in the unit, including how to handle a small number of clusters.

Threat

Source: Bellemare (2020), Section 5.2. This answers question 6.

Bellemare asks authors to discuss each threat in turn, say whether it applies, and explain how the paper handles it. The response column lists common approaches; it is not from Bellemare.
He adds: “If your results are not causally identified, do not lie about what they can and cannot do.”
The DAG from earlier shows each threat as a feature of the graph. The climate example later applies this table to one design.

title: Lecture 6.1: From Question to Estimating Equation
section: In the panel weather model, each threat has an answer
text:
In the panel weather model, each threat has an answer







Threat
In the panel weather model




Reverse causality
Farm output does not change the weather


Unobserved heterogeneity
County effects absorb fixed differences; year effects absorb national shocks


Measurement error
Gridded weather misses farm conditions; check a second weather data set


Spillovers
Year effects absorb national price changes, so the estimate excludes them



This applies question 6 to one design. Each row needs an answer: the threat does not apply, the design handles it, or a robustness check tests it.

The four threats are Bellemare’s list (Section 5.2): reverse causality, unobserved heterogeneity, measurement error, and spillovers. Dalheimer and Bellemare’s Section 2.2 (shown earlier) walks through the first three in this order, and the generic version is in the identification strategy section.
Classical measurement error in weather attenuates the estimate toward zero.
The record on this design shows why data checks matter: Fisher, Hanemann, Roberts, and Schlenker (2012) identified errors in the weather and climate data used by Deschênes and Greenstone, and Deschênes and Greenstone (2012) replied with corrected estimates.
